text: The United States military posting this video today saying the U.S. naval blockade against Iran remains in full effect.
They say as of July 25th, CENTCOM has redirected 12 commercial vessels trying to run the blockade,
also disabled two that didn't comply.
They boarded another two in order to ensure total compliance, they say.
Iran reported no U.S. strikes overnight.
Meanwhile, President Trump reportedly ordered the U.S. military not to conduct attacks on Friday, according to Axios.
This broke a 13-night streak of nightly strikes.
Despite a quieter past 24 hours, though, the United States has gradually expanded the scope of its attacks against Iran in recent weeks.
We, of course, saw President Trump at the White House Correspondents' Dinner talking late last night.
He was talking about some of the objectives in the war and some of the progress from the administration's standpoint.
President Trump says that he is weighing a massive attack on Iran, as the Wall Street Journal says,
the U.S. is surging forces toward the region in order to give Trump options to expand the war.
And according to Reuters, recent Iranian drone attacks on CIA facilities in the Gulf is making some question whether Russia is assisting the Iranians by providing targeting information.
Graham Slattery is here.
He's a White House correspondent in Washington focusing on national security, intelligence and foreign affairs.
Firstly, Graham, what's our level of knowledge about why the U.S. didn't strike last night?
Well, we can make a good inference.

Essentially, what we do know from our sourcing and from some of the reporting you referenced is that there was a fairly high-level meeting at the White House involving President Trump on Friday to discuss options.
And essentially, it was decided at that point, at least for now, not to hold off on a major expansion of operations for a number of reasons.
And one of the concerns is a lack of missile interceptors in the region.
So in that context, I think this reprieve makes a little bit of sense.
That's the context.
And did the Iranians strike last night from their vantage point?
The U.S. didn't.
But did the Iranians fire anything, to our knowledge?
To our knowledge, no.
Obviously, this war has mustasticized quite a bit.
So I don't want to rule out some sort of minor issue that perhaps we're not aware of.
However, I would note that the Yemeni Houthis did fire some projectiles at Saudi Arabia.
That's widely considered a proxy conflict that's related to this conflict, the Houthis being allied to Iran, the Saudis being allied with the United States.
And ultimately, the two, the Saudis and the Houthis, talk to us about the Bab al-Mendeb Strait.
Marine traffic brings us this live depiction of some of the traffic in that region.
We're so used to looking at the Strait of Hormuz.
But this whole other waterway, I mean, it's a critical passageway for global supply chains in its own right, Graham.
Explain to us the importance of the Bab al-Mendeb Strait and why we're tracking it so closely, especially as friction continues to rile up between the Saudis and the Houthis.
So this Strait is, you know, obviously we all learned a lot about the Strait of Hormuz in the last few months.
That was Iran's really their best choke point.
But they have further escalatory options on their side.
And one thing that they likely can do, certainly can try, likely can accomplish functionally is choking off this Strait, which is also, like this Strait of Hormuz, very vital for global commerce.
You obviously, you kind of have to go through this if you go through the Suez Canal.
So, you know, this is something that we all have to watch.
And it's something that President Trump is going to watch and the Republican Party as we head into, you know, the midterms.
Because if you can choke this off, it's going to make global prices rise.
So what do we know, moving back to the Strait of Hormuz and moving back to the direct conflict between the United States and Iran,
what do we know about what the U.S. is doing behind the scenes?
Obviously, we're not going to have all the details, but no strikes last night.
And President Trump has alluded to the fact that there could be some sort of bigger operation that they're working on.
What exactly should we be looking for?
And what exactly could the U.S. be preparing to do on their end?
So what's going on behind the scenes here?
You know, I'd say I'd separate this into two categories, military and intelligence.
They're building options, you know.
So they are surging various assets to the region, preparing for contingency plans, preparing for various options that President Trump could deploy,
you know, such as some sort of ground operation focused on a few Iranian nuclear sites,
a ground operation or some sort of bombing campaign focused on Karg Island, which is really crucial for Iranian oil exports.
It doesn't mean that the White House is going to actually deploy any of these options,
but they have to be ready at a moment's notice.
And we're, of course, seeing a lot of the U.S. intelligence agencies trying to define Iranian intentions,
what their weak points are, what the propensity for negotiations are.
So that's basically where we are at the moment.
You know, Graham, I was reading a lot of analysis about this over the past 24 hours or so,
especially in light of the 14th night not having any kinetic action.
Have the current level of strikes that the U.S. has been carrying out on Iran,
have that level of strikes basically reached their max level of effectiveness from the U.S. military's perspective?
In the view of the U.S. intelligence community largely, I think that's fair to say.
There has been some public reporting, you know, which I understand through our own channels to be accurate,
that various U.S. intelligence agencies, particularly the CIA and the DIA,
have assessed whether the current level of bombing will change Iran's strategic position
with respect to the nuclear program and negotiations.
And honestly, our intelligence analysts do not think that this level of bombing will move the needle.
So that's where we are.
It'll be something we have to watch closely in the coming days,
just to see what shape this conflict takes as time moves forward.
Before we go, I got to ask you about this.
You recently spoke to people familiar with U.S. intelligence who say that Iranian drone attacks
on CIA facilities in the Gulf have prompted the U.S. to investigate whether Russia is providing targeting information.
I don't believe, Graham, that it's completely news to us that the Russians might be aiding the Iranians
in some shape or form with this conflict.
But specifically with this report, what did you learn U.S. officials are looking into?
So multiple CIA facilities, and obviously their locations are clandestine,
but for our sourcing, multiple CIA facilities in the Middle East have been attacked by Iranian drones during this war.
There was one in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, one in eastern Iraq.
We believe there might be others.
And what CIA analysts are looking at in particular is whether these strikes on CIA facilities were aided by Russia.
We know that Russia has been aiding Iran generally,
but this would obviously be a very serious provocation to actually be helping essentially blow up CIA facilities
throughout the region.
And obviously it's concerning if they have all that information.
Graham Slattery is with Reuters.
We appreciate the time.
Have a good rest of your weekend.
Thanks.
You bet.
All right, let's step away for a quick commercial break, a live look at the White House.
We're back in about two minutes.
We'll be right back.
